questions.statement: I ___ my brother to fix the bike yesterday.
questions.context: The causative with have plus object plus bare infinitive.

options.feedback: Correct! The causative have plus object plus bare infinitive expresses an arrangement the speaker made.
The object pronoun must come before the bare infinitive, so the word order here is wrong.
Make plus object plus bare infinitive is possible, but the past of make is made and the sentence is about an arrangement.
A past continuous would describe an action under way, and the causative structure is needed here.

questions.explanation:
The causative have plus object plus bare infinitive says that someone arranged for the action to be done. The object comes first and the infinitive has no to.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She ___ the secretary to type the letter.
questions.context: The causative with get plus object plus to infinitive.

options.feedback: Correct! Get plus object plus to infinitive is a common causative form for arranging for someone to act.
With get the infinitive keeps its to, so the base form without to is wrong here.
Getten is not a form of get, whose past is got and whose participle is gotten or got.
A past continuous would describe an action under way and would lose the causative meaning.

questions.explanation:
Get plus object plus to infinitive is a causative structure with a slightly informal flavour. The to is required with get, unlike have.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The director ___ the students rewrite the essay.
questions.context: The causative with make plus object plus bare infinitive.

options.feedback: Correct! Make plus object plus bare infinitive expresses compulsion by the subject.
With make the infinitive never takes to, so to rewrite is wrong here.
Makes is the present form, and the sentence describes a past arrangement.
The -ing form is not the structure that make takes, which is the bare infinitive.

questions.explanation:
Make plus object plus bare infinitive says the subject compelled the action. It is a causative with a strong sense of obligation imposed from outside.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The tutor ___ the students work in pairs during the activity.
questions.context: The passive of the causative with let.

options.feedback: Correct! Let plus object plus bare infinitive expresses permission given by the subject.
With let the infinitive never takes to, so to work is wrong.
Lets is the present form, and the sentence describes a past permission.
Allow plus object plus to infinitive is also valid, but the infinitive keeps its to with allow.

questions.explanation:
Let plus object plus bare infinitive gives permission. It is the mirror image of make, since both take a bare infinitive and express a decision by the subject.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The roof ___ by a local company last month.
questions.context: The passive of the causative.

options.feedback: Correct! A past simple passive with by is the standard form for a repair arranged by somebody.
The active would make the roof the one doing the repairing, which is impossible.
A past continuous would suggest the repair was under way, and last month names a finished past time.
A past perfect would need a past point later than last month, and there is none.

questions.explanation:
Many causative sentences are naturally expressed in the passive, because the person who arranges the work is not the person who does it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: We ___ our windows cleaned before the visitors arrive.
questions.context: Have something done, where the speaker arranges the service.

options.feedback: Correct! Have plus object plus past participle means the speaker arranged for the work to be done.
A bare form after the object would make the subject the one doing the cleaning, which is not the meaning.
A past perfect would be the subject doing the cleaning, so the structure is the active not the causative.
Have to expresses obligation, and the infinitive or participle that follows it would be wrong.

questions.explanation:
Have plus object plus past participle is the most frequent causative in everyday English. It reports an arrangement rather than an action performed by the subject.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Can you help me ___ the boxes?
questions.context: Help plus to infinitive, which is correct in standard English.

options.feedback: Correct! Help plus to infinitive is the standard form in careful written English.
A bare infinitive after help is common in speech but is considered informal in standard written English.
The -ing form after help is not the standard structure, though it appears informally.
A that clause with help would need a different verb, and the infinitive is the usual form.

questions.explanation:
Help somebody to do something is the safest form for exams and formal writing. Help somebody do is widely used in conversation but is often marked down.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: By the time we arrived, the technician ___ the alarm ___.
questions.context: The causative with get in the past perfect, since the arrangement was complete.

options.feedback: Correct! The causative past perfect reports that the installation was arranged and complete before the arrival.
A present perfect would leave the installation inside the present period, ignoring the arrival deadline.
A past continuous would suggest the work was still under way when the visitors arrived.
The to infinitive would change the meaning from an arrangement to an obligation.

questions.explanation:
The causative behaves like any other verb for tense, so the arrangement can be reported in any tense. The structure of the two following elements never changes.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The company ___ a courier ___ the documents every Friday.
questions.context: Have someone do, in the present.

options.feedback: Correct! Have plus object plus bare infinitive in the present describes a regular arrangement.
The to infinitive would turn the sentence into a statement about the company's own obligation.
Have is the plural or first person auxiliary, and the subject is the singular company.
A continuous would describe a single action under way, not a weekly arrangement.

questions.explanation:
A regular arrangement with another agent is expressed with has plus object plus bare infinitive. Every Friday is what makes it a routine rather than one event.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: We watched him ___ the experiment from the window.
questions.context: The verb watch, which takes object plus bare infinitive.

options.feedback: Correct! Watch, see, hear, feel and make take a bare infinitive after the object.
These perception verbs do not take a to infinitive after the object, unlike help and get.
The -ing form follows watch as a different structure, not as its object complement.
Ran would make the main clause the past simple, but the object clause needs a base form.

questions.explanation:
A group of verbs takes object plus bare infinitive: make, let, have, see, hear, watch, feel and help. Only have in this group also allows a past participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I ___ my car ___ yet, so I am taking the bus.
questions.context: The negative form of a causative with have.

options.feedback: Correct! The negative sits after have and the participle closes the structure.
Did would place the arrangement in a finished past moment, and yet keeps the period open.
A present continuous would describe an arrangement under way, and the -ing complement is wrong.
After have as a causative the following verb must be a past participle, not a bare infinitive.

questions.explanation:
In have something done, the participle is obligatory. The structure reports that the work was arranged, whether or not it has been carried out.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The manager ___ the new employee ___ the system last week.
questions.context: Get someone to do, in the past.

options.feedback: Correct! Get plus object plus to infinitive in the past describes an arrangement that was made.
With get the infinitive keeps its to, so the bare form is wrong in this structure.
Getten is not the past simple of get, which is got.
A past continuous would describe the manager in the act of arranging, which is not the reported event.

questions.explanation:
Get plus object plus to infinitive is the informal counterpart of have plus object plus bare infinitive. Both report an arrangement, and they differ only in the presence of to.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ you ___ your hair cut before the ceremony?
questions.context: The question form of a causative.

options.feedback: Correct! Have plus object plus past participle in a question keeps the have before the subject.
Did builds active tenses and cannot carry the causative structure.
The to infinitive would change the meaning from an arrangement to the subject's own obligation.
A passive continuous would not express the arrangement the question is about.

questions.explanation:
A causative question in the present is simply have before the subject, with the object and the participle after. The verb have does the work of the auxiliary.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Would you ___ me carry this table upstairs?
questions.context: The verb help used without an object.

options.feedback: Correct! Help plus object plus to infinitive is the standard structure, and the question word order is unchanged by it.
The -ing form after would would make the sentence a passive or an adjective, and it cannot follow a modal directly.
Helped after would is not a valid form, because the modal carries the tense.
A that clause would need a different verb, and help takes an infinitive rather than a clause.

questions.explanation:
Help is one of the verbs that keeps its to when it takes an object. Would you help me to carry is the form that is safe in every register.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "I will have the car serviced tomorrow," she said. She said that she ___ have the car serviced the next day.
questions.context: A causative in a reported statement, where the auxiliary shifts.

options.feedback: Correct! The will of the original future auxiliary backshifts to would in the report.
Keeping will would ignore the past tense of the reporting verb she said.
A had would report a past perfect, and the original is a future arrangement.
Be going to is a different future form and does not correspond to the will of the original sentence.

questions.explanation:
A causative clause backshifts exactly like any other future verb. The rest of the causative structure, have the car serviced, is untouched by the shift.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She persuaded him ___ to the trip.
questions.context: The verb persuade with a to infinitive.

options.feedback: Correct! Persuade somebody to do something uses a to infinitive for the person who is persuaded.
The -ing form is not the structure after persuade somebody, which needs a to infinitive.
To plus -ing is not a possible combination in English.
A that clause would require a different verb such as convince, and persuade takes an infinitive.

questions.explanation:
Persuade somebody to do, advise somebody to do and tell somebody to do all use a to infinitive. Convince somebody that plus clause is the alternative structure.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: His parents made him ___ late to school. They would not let him ___ out.
questions.context: The negative causative with make.

options.feedback: Correct! With make and let the infinitive is bare, so a negative form places not before the whole infinitive.
The to infinitive is not the structure that make and let take.
English does not negate an infinitive with not after the verb, and go not is not a possible form.
Going is the -ing form, and let plus object plus -ing is not the structure being used.

questions.explanation:
When the complement of make or let is negative, the not stands in front of the whole infinitive: made him not be, would not let him go.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The office ___ every evening, so the building is always empty at night.
questions.context: A service arranged in the past, reported in the passive.

options.feedback: Correct! An unspecified doer reported in the past takes the past simple passive.
The active would make the office the one doing the cleaning, which is not possible.
A present passive would describe a routine, and the sentence reports a past fact.
A past perfect would need a later past reference point, and the sentence is a general statement.

questions.explanation:
A cleaning service described as a regular past arrangement is naturally passive, because the people who do the work are not identified.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I ___ my flat last weekend. It took me two days.
questions.context: The causative where the speaker did the work themselves.

options.feedback: Correct! With a reflexive object the causative collapses into a plain past form, because no other agent is involved.
A past perfect would place the painting before another past point, and last weekend is the only past time here.
The last part is not part of the verb, and the sentence would have no main verb.
A present perfect would place the painting inside the present period, and it is finished.

questions.explanation:
When the subject arranges for themselves to do the work, the causative disappears. I painted my flat is a normal active sentence, not a causative.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He ___ his watch ___ at the jeweller's.
questions.context: The verb get something done, which reports an arrangement.

options.feedback: Correct! Get plus object plus past participle reports that the repair was arranged.
With get plus object the structure is a past participle, and to repair would report an obligation instead.
Getten is not the past simple of get, which is got.
A past continuous would describe the arranging as under way, and the sentence reports it as done.

questions.explanation: Get plus object plus past participle is the passive-side causative. It says the subject arranged for the work, without saying who actually carried it out.
questions.subject: ingles
